As one of the 19th century’s foremost painters of everyday life—scenes of regular people in cafés, railways, bars and more—the famed French modernist Édouard Manet defied tradition and found inspiration in the gritty, unvarnished streets of major European cities.

One of his largest paintings, The Old Musician (1862), embodies this ethos at a scale usually reserved for famous or historical figures. The eight-foot-wide frame is filled with an aging violinist surrounded by a varied crowd—a barefoot girl clutching an infant, two young boys, a top-hatted ragpicker and a turbaned older man—all of whom, in an effort to highlight the humanity of the marginalized, are brought to the fore.

“We are not accustomed to seeing such simple and direct translations of reality,” the French novelist Émile Zola remarked of Manet’s paintings in 1867, according to a translation by the Royal Academy of Arts. “Then, as I said, there is such a surprisingly elegant awkwardness ... it is a truly charming experience to contemplate this luminous and serious painting which interprets nature with a gentle brutality.”

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/RZkL3NLOy5UJg4-S-Bh5xWNFDVk=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(566x453:567x454)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/f3/6e/f36e2a36-584e-42ba-9727-42c738cf666e/edouard_manet_pflasterer_in_der_rue_mosnier.jpg

Researchers believe that The Old Musician, on display at the National Gallery of Art, in Washington, D.C., was inspired by the people Manet encountered outside his Paris studio. In the 1860s, the neighborhood was razed at the order of Emperor Napoleon III to pave new boulevards.
Now, a rediscovered drawing sheds possible new light on the history of the painting’s creation.

As was first reported by the Guardian’s Dalya Alberge, the small red-chalk sketch, long held in a private art collection in northern Italy, has been newly attributed to Manet. The drawing, spotted recently by art historian Francesco Baccanelli, is believed to be a study for The Old Musician. It depicts a crouching young girl who resembles both the girl in that painting and a woman, bent in a similar pose, in another Manet work, Le Déjeuner sur l’Herbe (1863).

Le Déjeuner sur l’Herbe was rejected by the jury of the 1863 Paris Salon for flouting conventions of perspective, composition and propriety.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/wfupK6A1Nce0Za7KR9iDUIR8l9U=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(480x375:481x376)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/4e/a8/4ea81757-e11e-4795-8bcc-f1dd051a6fad/edouard_manet_-_luncheon_on_the_grass_-_google_art_project.jpg

“It just felt like: ‘Oh gosh, that’s exciting,’” Emily Beeny, a museum curator and leading Manet expert, who received photographs of the drawing from Baccanelli, tells the Guardian. “Lots of people send me things they imagine might be by Manet, but this is the only one so far that has given me an immediate sense of recognition. I’m not sure when the last unpublished drawing by Manet was discovered, but it has definitely been many years.”

The chalk drawing is similar to others attributed to Manet, and historians have discerned some of the artist’s signature styles, such as “the abrupt transitions between light and shadow, and the peculiar plump, tapered fingers—little figural tics that are very characteristic of Manet,” Beeny tells the outlet. An ultraviolet analysis of the roughly 8-by-7-inch sketch also revealed evidence of the artist’s studio stamp in its right-hand corner.

But the drawing also poses new questions, especially for experts less confident about its ties to existing works. The key detail is the box Manet drew around the child, an example of “squaring,” which typically indicates that the artist was pleased with the work and intended to transfer it to canvas. But the portrait of the crouching girl doesn’t exist in any Manet painting.

“The sketch may have been intended for the Finding of Moses, a major unfinished painting Manet worked on in the late 1850s that was eventually cut down and turned into The Surprised Nymph (1861),” Artnet’s Richard Whiddington writes.

As for the identity of the child, Beeny and Baccanelli speculate that—even though the sketch seems to show a girl—Manet may have turned to a young boy named Alexandre, who cleaned his brushes and workspace, for inspiration. The two experts have written a full scholarly review of the drawing and its links to Manet and his work for the forthcoming October issue of the Burlington Magazine, a monthly art journal.
